sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? No.** The headline "Notes from the boat shed" (about x 100–730, y 95–145) sounds like a diary entry, and the whole left column (x 100–585, y 200–305) is scene-setting. The real purpose only shows up in the right column (x 670–1145, y 200–305): come and volunteer. Even there it is incomplete. "Thursday evenings" gives no start time, "the end of the lane" names no lane or town, and there is no contact, sign-up or link. So a newcomer finishes reading with a nice picture of the shed and still can't say where to go, when, or who to tell. That breaks Krug's point that a page should make clear within seconds what it is and what you can do (*Don't Make Me Think*). Fix: let the headline or a standfirst under it say this is an invitation, for example something like "Help us restore three dinghies on Thursday nights". Then give the ask the facts a person needs to act on: day, time, address, and who to contact or "just turn up". Defect. Weight: major, if the job is recruiting volunteers as I assume. If the page is meant only as a mood piece, this becomes minor.

**What's working.**
- Everything looks like one thing. A single bold serif headline, matching serif body text and near-black on white give it a quiet, homely, hand-kept feel that suits a volunteer boat shed. There are no stray boxes, rules or ornaments.
- The concrete details in the copy ("three clinker dinghies", "tar and cut cedar", "a kettle on, and a spare apron on the hook") make the place feel real and welcoming. "Nobody needs experience" removes the main reason people hold back. Keep all of it when the logistics are added.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The bottom 60% of the frame (y ~310–800) is empty. It could be the end of the page, or more content (a map, a sign-up form, contact details) that didn't load or sits below the fold. If the missing facts from finding 1 are down there, it becomes a hierarchy and placement problem rather than missing content. Check this in a live browser.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (first-time viewer can say in one sentence what it is for).

**Walk (working notes).** The image is about 1280×800, roughly one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the crop script.

First read: the eye lands on the bold serif headline "Notes from the boat shed" (y≈90–145). It then drops to the left column and moves across to the right. It reads as a calm, editorial page for a small community boat-restoration group. The page looks unfinished, because the lower 60% is empty.

Job (my assumption): a short page that introduces a volunteer boat shed and invites people to join.

What matters first:
- One element clearly dominates: yes. The headline looks about 3× the body size and much heavier.
- Each level is distinct from the next, with no near-duplicate sizes: yes. There are only two levels, title and body, and the gap between them is large.
- Headings differ in more than size: yes. The headline is bold and the body is regular, in the same serif.

Every line is yes, so there is no step 5 deep read.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One clear focal point.** The headline (x≈100–730, y≈90–145) looks about 3× the body size and is set in a heavy bold. Nothing else on the page competes with it, so the eye knows where to start straight away.
- **Contrast from more than size.** The title and body use the same serif. Only the size and the bold-versus-regular weight separate them, and together those make two levels you can tell apart instantly. The step is large and nothing sits in between, so the hierarchy looks deliberate. Keep that two-level discipline if subheads are added later: any new level should be clearly between the two, not close to either.

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. Everything on the page sits in one band from y≈90 to y≈305: the headline, then two four-line columns. The 1280×800 frame below that, about 490 px or 60% of the height, is empty. The bottom of the frame holds nothing, so the page looks top-heavy and unfinished, as if a section failed to load or the copy ran out. It doesn't look like it was laid out to sit in this frame. Here the empty space is what's left after the content ends, not something placed against it, so it gives the dense band nothing to push against. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says a heavy area needs a counterweight. Fix: either give the lower field something to carry, such as a picture of the shed, the Thursday time and place, or a way to sign up, or crop or size the frame to the content so the text block sits in the page on purpose. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.** The two text columns share one grid. The left column lines up exactly with the headline at x≈100, the gutter is ≈70 px, and both columns run on the same baselines (≈211/239/267/295), so they read as one calm, matched pair. The headline also sits close enough above the columns to own them clearly.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The blank lower 60% may be content that hadn't loaded yet, or a page that continues below an 800 px viewport. Check the live page. If more content follows, the balance finding becomes a question about the first screen only.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances).

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies (one heading and two body paragraphs set in two columns).

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The body text is easy to read.** The type looks about 17 px with roughly 28 px between lines. The left column's lines run about 55 to 60 characters ("The shed sits at the end of the lane, where the tide comes"), which sits inside Bringhurst's 45 to 75 range. The spacing between lines suits that length, so the eye finds the next line easily. Dark text on white is clearly above 4.5:1. Keep the column width and line spacing if the layout changes.
- **The heading and body read as one plan.** It looks like one serif family: a heavy bold for the heading (about 60 px, one line) and the regular weight for the text. The contrast comes from size and weight alone, with no second face competing. The heading's letter pairs ("Notes", "from", "boat shed") look evenly spaced. Neither column ends on a single stranded word, and both ragged right edges are gently uneven, with no staircase or wedge.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

First read: the eye goes straight to the bold headline at the top left (about 100–730 × 90–145), then drops to the two body columns. It reads as a short community or club note about a boat-restoration shed, and it feels calm, plain and bookish. Job (my assumption): an informal page inviting volunteers.

Walk, Color:
- Small palette: yes. Only near-black and dark slate on white, with no other hue.
- Strong colour kept to a small share: yes. There is no saturated colour.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white, and the structure holds in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. Nothing relies on colour temperature.
- Matching colours look the same: yes.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colours used for their meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. Colour carries no meaning here.
- Dark theme background: yes. This is a light theme.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The colour is near-monochrome, dark type on white.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** Colour stays out of the way. The headline (about x 100–730, y 90–145) is a dark slate that is a little cooler and softer than pure black, and the body text is near-black. Both sit on plain white with strong contrast, so the page's structure comes from size and weight, not from colour. It reads cleanly in grayscale and suits a quiet, text-only note.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon or other picture, only a headline and two text columns.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Below the text, from about y≈320 to the bottom at y=800, the frame is blank white. That is roughly the lower 60% of a 1280×800 image. On a page called "Notes from the boat shed", that space may be where a photo of the shed or the dinghies was supposed to go and didn't load when the screenshot was taken. Open the page in a live browser to see whether an image belongs there. If one does, it should be critiqued under pictures. If not, the empty space belongs to the arrangement critic.
